title: “Software is over”: Bold AI developer takes aim at Adobe with open source clones
gist: Developer Brandon Thomas used Claude Opus 5.5 to build seven open source, Rust-based clones of Adobe's Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat Pro under the Artcraft brand, claiming near-full parity within months. Ars notes the apps are an alpha with shortcomings and possible trade-dress legal risk, but Thomas argues AI makes cloning paid software trivial.

insights.claim: Artcraft pivoted from a controllable AI image and video editing tool to a suite of seven open source apps recreating the interface and tools of Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign and Acrobat Pro.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: A small team is directly targeting Adobe's entire Creative Suite, putting pressure on subscription incumbents.
insights.locator: Artcraft got its start last year

insights.claim: Brandon Thomas says he used Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 to build 'clean-room replacements' in Rust, with WebAssembly versions for browsers, and has coded exclusively with AI tools since February.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: AI coding agents are now credible enough for one developer to attempt replicating decades-old professional software.
insights.locator: In announcing those new apps on Reddit

insights.claim: Commenters on Hacker News and elsewhere point out many current shortcomings, and the software is in a 'super early alpha' state.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Functional parity claims are unproven; early quality is the main test of the thesis.
insights.locator: And while commenters on Hacker News

insights.claim: Thomas initially promised 100 percent feature parity within a month, then revised on Hacker News to say 99 percent parity will take a while, measured in months rather than years.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The timeline slipped within days, which signals overconfidence and a need to discount the claim.
insights.quote: “We’re going to reach 100% [feature] parity within a month,”

insights.claim: Thomas says he was motivated by being bitten by Adobe's dark-pattern cancellation fees one too many times.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Subscription friction and cancellation fees are a customer-resentment vector that fuels substitution.
insights.locator: Thomas, who says he has about a decade

insights.claim: The free MIT/Apache-licensed apps are to be funded by selling token-based access to the existing Artcraft visual AI model and IDE, offered inside the apps alongside third-party models, and by a team building software for filmmakers.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: The model is free software as a funnel for paid AI generation tokens, rather than seat licenses.
insights.locator: Development of the totally free options

insights.claim: Reverse engineering that replicates functionality without copying code is generally legally acceptable, but the apps could face trouble if their trade dress too closely mimics Adobe's appearance and interface.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: Look-and-feel copying, not code, is the main legal exposure for AI-built clones.
insights.locator: Thomas is the latest in a long line

insights.claim: Thomas argues everyday developers can soon recreate open source versions of popular paid software, claiming 'Software is over', and says he will replace Google Search, build smartphones and de-enshittify tech.
insights.speaker: Kyle Orland
insights.so_what: If AI makes functional cloning cheap, paid software moats weaken, though this view is a boast from an alpha-stage developer.
insights.quote: “Software is over,” he gloated in an earlier comment, claiming to have “one-shotted Photoshop. The whole thing.”
